text: Alkaff Mansion and the Alkaffs: A Hadhrami Family on Telok Blangah Hill
On top of Telok Blangah Hill, above Keppel Harbour, stands a white two-storey house with a red-tiled roof and a small clock tower.
It was built around 1918 as a weekend retreat by the Alkaffs, an Arab family whose fortune began with trade in spices, sugar and coffee.
The family came from the Hadhramaut, a long desert valley in what is now Yemen, and for a few decades it owned some of the best-known landmarks in Singapore.
The Alkaffs were sayyids, a family that traces its descent to the Prophet Muhammad, from the town of Tarim in the Hadhramaut.
For centuries, men from the valley had sailed out to the ports of the Indian Ocean to trade, and many of them settled in the Malay world.
According to the National Heritage Board, the founder of the family firm, Syed Shaik bin Abdul Rahman Alkaff, came to Singapore from the Hadhramaut in 1852.
His firm, Alkaff and Company, traded in spices, sugar, coffee and textiles between India and the Dutch East Indies, and it put much of its profit into land.
By the turn of the 20th century the Alkaffs were among the largest property owners in Singapore, alongside two other Hadhrami families, the Alsagoffs and the Aljunieds.
I wrote about one of the Alsagoffs in an earlier post.
Like many Hadhrami merchants, the family kept close ties with home, and a good deal of the money made in Singapore went back to the valley.
In Tarim, the Alkaffs built a cluster of large mud-brick palaces, which are still the town's grandest houses.
One of the family, Sayyid Abubakr bin Shaikh Alkaff, was born in Singapore around 1890 and later settled in the Hadhramaut.
He paid for a school and a hospital in Tarim and helped finance a road from the interior to the coast.
In 1936 he helped the British official Harold Ingrams broker a truce between the valley's warring Qu'aiti and Kathiri states.
The family's best-known building in town was the Alkaff Arcade, which opened on Collyer Quay on the 27th of November 1909.
It was designed by the architect David McLeod Craik of Swan and Maclaren in a Moorish style, with two onion domes at the corners.
Inside, a covered passage ran from Raffles Square through to the waterfront, lined with shops on the ground floor and offices above.
The Straits Times called it "possibly the most unique" of the city's new buildings, and it is often described as Singapore's first indoor shopping centre.
The Arcade replaced the old office and godowns of the trading firm Guthrie and Company.
The first tenants included the shipping line P&O and the oil company Standard Oil, and Alkaff and Company kept its own office in the building.
At the opening luncheon, according to the Straits Times, the chronicler Charles Burton Buckley gave the speech on behalf of Syed Shaik, who did not speak English.
The family also owned, for a time, the Hotel de l'Europe, one of the city's grand hotels, on the site where the old Supreme Court building now stands.
Around 1930, the head of the family, Syed Abdul Rahman bin Shaikh Alkaff, opened a park on his land off Upper Serangoon Road.
He brought in a Japanese landscape gardener, and the result, the Alkaff Lake Gardens, is said to have been Singapore's first Japanese-style garden.
It had a man-made lake with boats and fishing, artificial hills, Japanese bridges and tea houses, and in the 1930s it was a popular place for an evening or a weekend out.
Nearby, on his land, he paid for a mosque.
The Alkaff Upper Serangoon Mosque opened on the 24th of June 1932, with a slender Ottoman-style minaret and a prayer hall of Moorish horseshoe arches.
It was made a national monument in 2014.
That same year, 1932, another member of the family, Syed Ahmad Alkaff, helped pay for a mosque at Kampung Melayu, near Kaki Bukit.
It was rebuilt in the 1990s and still carries the family name.
The hill above Telok Blangah was then known as Mount Washington, possibly because of the family's close ties with Singapore's small American community.
A member of the family bought the land in 1916, and the house was finished around 1918.

In 1989 the Straits Times credited it to Syed Abdulrahman Alkaff, who was born in the Hadhramaut in 1867 and came to Singapore late in the 19th century, though some accounts name other members of the family.
It was a weekend house, not a home, and the Alkaffs used it to entertain.
Through the 1920s and 1930s the newspapers reported receptions and parties there.
In 1930 a group of young Arabs hosted Malay footballers at the house, and in 1936 the Chinese Consul-General held a reception there for a visiting general from China.
In December 1941, as war reached Malaya, the British military took over the Alkaff Lake Gardens, and a volunteer ambulance unit made its headquarters there.
A large Red Cross sign was laid out on the grass, but after the unit left, the gardens were bombed and shelled, and during the Japanese occupation they were closed to the public.
Syed Abdul Rahman himself was kept out of his own park.
After the war, the family's fortunes faded.
Rent control, which from 1947 held many rents at their pre-war levels, cut into the income of landlords like the Arab families.
Syed Abdul Rahman bin Shaikh Alkaff died in Tarim in August 1948.
In July 1950 the gardens were sold to the Sennett Realty Company, which planned a housing estate of about 1,400 houses for some 10,000 people on the land around them.
The Straits Times reported that the lake would be filled in, and readers wrote in asking for the park to be saved.
The lake survived until 1964, when it was drained and the land was cleared for new schools.
Cedar Girls' Secondary School stands on the site today.
The Arcade was sold in 1973 and pulled down in March 1978 to make way for the office tower that now carries its name.
The house on Mount Washington stood empty for years after the war, and a Buddhist organisation is reported to have used it in the 1970s and early 1980s.
In the late 1980s, the house was restored as part of a plan to make the hill a tourist attraction, and in September 1990 it opened as a restaurant.
Its interior was fitted out in the style of a rich Singapore home of the 1920s and 1930s, and its speciality was the rijsttafel, the Dutch-Indonesian "rice table" of many small dishes.
At the sound of a gong, a line of women in kebayas came out of the kitchen, each carrying a dish.
When I was working at Security Pacific, I went to a lunch at Alkaff Mansion.
It was a slightly more expensive place, and brokers loved a chance to spend money on their clients.
It was cooler up there than down in town, because the house sits higher up.
I have wanted to go back, but it is out of the way now that I no longer drive in Singapore.
The restaurant closed in 2003, and the house stood empty again for eight years.
It was given conservation status in 2005, reopened as an Italian restaurant in December 2011, and closed again in 2016.
Since 2019, the mansion has been run by the restaurant group 1-Group, with a Spanish restaurant, a bar called the 1918 Heritage Bar, and a café.
It is also a popular place for weddings.
The family name is still on the map.
Besides the mansion and the two mosques, a new Alkaff Lake opened in Bidadari Park on the 3rd of September 2024, about 500 metres north of where the old lake was.
It is 1.8 hectares in size and doubles as a flood-control pond for the new Bidadari housing estate, whose newest neighbourhood is also named after the Alkaffs.

Where it fits in the bigger story: The Alkaffs were one of a small number of Hadhrami families who helped build colonial Singapore, and whose money also built schools, roads and palaces in a desert valley thousands of kilometres away.
Most of their landmarks have gone, but their name has outlived them, on two mosques, a new lake and a house on a hill that most visitors know only as a place to eat.
